Bulkheads: The front and rear sections of the aircraft are calculated as semi-circles based on the cabin width. Cargo Holds (Fore, Aft, and Bulk): The total surface area of the cargo holds in an aircraft is determined by converting the cargo hold volume into a surface area. Calculation and Source: Volume capacity data can be found in tables of general aircraft characteristics. Each cargo hold volume should be calculated separately. Exclusions: All calculations are based solely on usable capacity. Certain characteristics, such as water volume, may be stated but should not be used for consistency. Aircraft with optional auxiliary fuel tanks may have variable cargo hold volumes. It is assumed that such optional tanks are not installed, and the maximum cargo volume is used. Some characteristics may combine the total capacity of all holds. The section on loading combinations provides a breakdown of how loads are distributed in the holds. For example, one LD3 is a standard air container model. Although this calculation may result in a slightly smaller area, the difference is negligible at the scale being calculated. Freighters and Double-Deck Commercial Aircraft: The area of freighters is calculated similarly to regular commercial aircraft, with the exception that the area error ratio is set to 1 because freighters lack linings, bulkheads, or overhead compartments. For double-deck commercial aircraft, such as the Boeing 747 and Airbus A380, the upper deck calculations must be added to the cabin floor area. This includes the upper deck cabin length multiplied by its width. Double-deck aircraft have two levels of overhead lockers, although the bulkhead and lining areas are similar to those of single-deck commercial aircraft like the Boeing 737-800. Example Calculation: For a Boeing 737-800, data on aircraft characteristics can be sourced from the manufacturer’s website. Disinsection Spray Requirements: To achieve a 2% permethrin emulsion, mix one part of a 50% permethrin EC formulation with 24 parts water (e.g., 42 mL of permethrin 50% EC per 1 liter of water). For cabin walls, ceilings, or cargo holds, apply 10 mL of permethrin per square meter. Residual Spray Application: Residual spray amounts are specified for effective treatment when mixed and applied correctly. For example, the floor is sprayed twice with a 10 mL solution (totaling 20 mL), with an additional 5 mL accounting for assumed drift from higher areas. Spray Application in Aircraft: Operators use aerosol cans to spray the cabin and cargo areas systematically. For example, in a Boeing 747, operators start at the rear of the aircraft and move forward at a rate of one step or one row of seats per second, directing the spray toward open overhead lockers. For double-deck aircraft, the upper deck is treated similarly, ensuring all stowage compartments are open during treatment. Post-Spraying Protocol: After spraying, the aircraft must remain closed for five minutes before reopening and resuming air-conditioning and flight preparations. Cargo hold doors should be opened only enough to introduce the aerosol can and must be closed immediately after spraying. Spray Amounts by Aircraft Type: Minimum aerosol spray amounts are specified for different aircraft models, including commercial passenger aircraft, freighters, and military aircraft. For example, a Boeing 737-800 requires 80 grams of permethrin 2% for pre-embarkation cabin treatment and additional amounts for forward and aft holds. Residual Disinsection Certification: Updated standards and recommended practices for aircraft disinsection are outlined in Annex 9 of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidelines.
